subChunks.title: Jackson: Mapping Java Objects to JSON
subChunks.hookHtml: When your Java application talks to a REST API, data leaves as JSON and arrives as JSON. Jackson is the library that converts Java objects to JSON strings (serialisation) and JSON strings back to Java objects (deserialisation). Every Spring Boot application uses it by default.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is Serialisation?

  • Serialisation: Java object → JSON string (for sending over the network or writing to a file)
  • Deserialisation: JSON string → Java object (for reading data that arrived from outside)

Jackson ObjectMapper

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();

// Serialise (object → JSON string)
Spell spell = new Spell("Fireball", 80);
String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(spell);
// → {"name":"Fireball","damage":80}

// Pretty print
String pretty = mapper.writerWithDefaultPrettyPrinter()
                      .writeValueAsString(spell);

// Deserialise (JSON string → object)
String input = "{\"name\":\"Frostbolt\",\"damage\":120}";
Spell parsed = mapper.readValue(input, Spell.class);
System.out.println(parsed.getName()); // Frostbolt

POJO Requirements for Jackson

By default, Jackson maps fields via public getters/setters. Your class needs:

  1. A no-argument constructor (Jackson uses it to create the object before setting fields)
  2. Public getters for each field you want serialised
  3. Public setters for each field you want deserialised into

Key Annotations

@JsonProperty("spell_name")  // map to a different JSON key
private String name;

@JsonIgnore                  // exclude this field from JSON
private String internalSecret;

@JsonAlias({"dmg", "power"}) // accept multiple JSON keys for one field
private int damage;

Collections and Nested Objects

// List of objects
List<Spell> spells = mapper.readValue(jsonArray,
    new TypeReference<List<Spell>>() {});

// Nested object — just works if Spell contains a Mage field
class Spell {
    private String name;
    private Mage caster;  // Jackson recurses into nested objects automatically
}

storyBeats.text: The Academy's inter-tower messaging system transmits spell data not as objects, but as plain text strings that any system can read. The translation layer is called Jackson.

storyBeats.speaker: Data Scribe Mira
storyBeats.text: When your Java object needs to travel over the network, it must become a string. JSON is the universal format. Jackson handles the conversion in both directions — serialise means object to JSON; deserialise means JSON to object. The ObjectMapper is the engine for both.

storyBeats.speaker: Serialise and deserialise a Spell
Data Scribe Mira
storyBeats.text: Jackson's defaults work automatically for public getters and setters. When the JSON key doesn't match your field name, use @JsonProperty to remap. When you need to hide a field from JSON output — a password, an internal ID — use @JsonIgnore. When an external API sends a field under multiple possible names, @JsonAlias accepts all of them.

learningObjectives: Use ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString() to serialise a Java object to a JSON string
Use ObjectMapper.readValue() to deserialise a JSON string into a Java object
Deserialise a JSON array into a List<T> using TypeReference
commonMistakes: Forgetting a no-argument constructor on the target class — Jackson cannot instantiate it without one
Using private fields with no getters and not configuring ObjectMapper to access them — fields won't be serialised
Catching JsonProcessingException with a broad Exception catch — you lose the specific error message
Using ObjectMapper.readValue() with the wrong target class — produces incorrect mapping silently or throws
assessmentCriteria: Can write a POJO that Jackson can serialise/deserialise without configuration
Can use @JsonProperty to map a field to a differently-named JSON key
Can deserialise a JSON array string into a List<MyClass>
Can explain why a missing no-arg constructor causes Jackson to throw at runtime
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain JSON serialisation and deserialisation to a teammate. What does Jackson need from a class to map it? What does @JsonIgnore do? When would you use TypeReference?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Create a Spell POJO with fields name (String), tier (String), and damage (int). Use Jackson to:

  1. Serialise a Spell with name "Blizzard", tier "SENIOR", damage 250 to a JSON string and print it
  2. Deserialise the JSON string {"name":"Frostbolt","tier":"JUNIOR","damage":120} back into a Spell and print its name and damage
  3. Add @JsonProperty("spell_damage") to the damage field and verify the output key changes
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From scratch. Create a Mage class with: id (int), name (String), school (String), and secretCode (String, annotated @JsonIgnore). Serialise a Mage and verify secretCode does NOT appear in the JSON. Then deserialise this JSON string: [{"id":1,"name":"Lyria","school":"Fire"},{"id":2,"name":"Vey","school":"Ice"}] into a List<Mage> using TypeReference and print the name of each mage.

questions.prompt: Which Jackson annotation excludes a field from both serialisation and deserialisation?
questions.explanation: @JsonIgnore tells Jackson to skip the annotated field entirely — it won't appear in the JSON output and won't be populated during deserialisation. Use it for sensitive fields like passwords or internal implementation details.

questions.prompt: A developer creates a Jackson POJO with all private fields but no getters. What happens when they try to serialise it?
options: Jackson serialises all private fields by reflection automatically
The JSON output is an empty object {}
questions.answer: The JSON output is an empty object {}
questions.explanation: By default Jackson accesses fields through public getters. With no getters and no special configuration, it finds nothing to serialise and produces an empty object. Fix: add public getters, or configure mapper.setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.FIELD, Visibility.ANY) to access fields directly.
